prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a new measurement capability in the strict sense: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the trade-off between long interrogation and perturbation by the trap, and Ye's group then showed what the idea could deliver, with many-body clocks, systematic budgets near 1e-18 and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. The result has been confirmed independently at JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and elsewhere, the accuracy budgets are agreed across laboratories, and the technique is already central to the preparation for a redefinition of the SI second, to relativistic geodesy and to bounds on drifting constants. That is a discovery-by-instrument that is mature, demonstrably lasting and cleanly attributable to two people. Five of eight members ranked it, three of them first, and it is the only shortlisted candidate with both strong first-place support and an uncontested two-name allocation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that metrology prizes are a repeated pattern (the 2005 comb prize to Hall and Hansch, the earlier laser-cooling and clock awards), so the committee may see this as an incremental refinement of an already-honoured toolkit rather than a new physical phenomenon. Mehlig ranked it only sixth, and the criteria ask for a discovery or invention, so I must be able to say what is new beyond better numbers. Attribution also leaves open Lemonde, Derevianko and the Ludlow-Hinkley experimental teams, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the operational payoff is still prospective.

responses.point: Olsson puts twisted bilayer graphene first, because Bistritzer-MacDonald told the community where to look and the 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity, with a coherent three-person configuration.
responses.response: I ranked B047 third myself and accept that its importance and breadth are very large. My doubt is about maturity, not significance: the superconducting mechanism is still unsettled and the field is only eight years old. A prize for the clocks rests on results whose interpretation is closed. I also want her view on the attribution, since the experimental credit sits with Jarillo-Herrero as group leader while Cao and Fatemi, who made the measurements, are outside the credited names. If that can be defended I would move B047 up, but I would not put it ahead of B019 this year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active-matter hydrodynamics first as a clean universal mechanism (Vicsek flocking, Toner-Tu, Ramaswamy) and ranks the clocks only sixth, noting that they sit close in spirit to earlier metrology prizes and that the frequency comb was already recognised in 2005.
responses.response: The overlap with 2005 is a fair challenge, but the comb is a ruler for optical frequencies and the lattice clock is a different invention: a way of making the atoms themselves an ideal reference with the trap shift cancelled. On B009, I value the universality of the idea but I cannot judge the experimental footing from my side. The strong support for flocking comes from quantitative scaling and a few experiments on bacteria and colloidal rollers, and with only one first-place vote it needs a broader constituency, plus a solution to the missing Yuhai Tu, before I could support it above a mature, multiply confirmed result like the clocks.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the physics of strong light-matter coupling on a chip, the standard architecture for superconducting qubits, and sees recognition as timely, perhaps slightly overdue.
responses.response: I take the physics argument seriously and I can see it is the right kind of discovery rather than a technology. My reservation is the timing: the 2025 prize went to macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which Kroll and Lindroth both flagged as close, and the attribution among Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf and the Yale programme (Girvin, Devoret) is harder than for the two-name clock case. Circuit QED has only three first-or-top-three votes spread across three members and is out of my expertise on the theory side, so I would hold it as a candidate for a later year rather than pair it with the clocks.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clocks first as a decisive step in measurement precision, with a clean two-person prize resting on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the Ye group's precision implementation.
responses.response: I agree with the allocation, and the Katori-Ye pair is how I would credit it. Where I add a qualification is on his second choice: Kroll, Lindroth and I all rank ultracold-atom quantum simulation highly, but the committee has already honoured BEC in 2001 and laser cooling in 1997 and 2018, and the Mott-transition paper is credited to a Munich team larger than the three names. I would keep B017 as the first alternative rather than combine it with the clocks, because a two-topic AMO prize would need a clear split of the three names and I do not see one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the clocks as a new invention or as a continuation of earlier metrology prizes, and how heavily the 2005 comb prize should weigh.
Whether Lemonde, Derevianko or the Ludlow-Hinkley teams have a stronger claim than the supplied credit allows.
Whether the twisted bilayer graphene case should wait for the superconducting mechanism to settle, and whether Bistritzer is the right third name beside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
How far the pending redefinition of the SI second should affect timing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known institutional or collaborative link to Katori, Ye, or any of the other shortlisted candidates; my own work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur is in astroparticle detectors and is unrelated to atomic clocks. I do rely on colleagues for atomic, condensed-matter and quantum-information physics.
